STOICHEIA / SAVED EXPERIMENT / EUCLID I.22

Three lengths. Can they close?

Α = 5.0, Β = 6.0, Γ = 4.0. Arbitrary drawing units. Construction step 5 of 5. Vertex chosen below the base.

Two crossings. A triangle on either side.

All three strict inequalities hold. Each crossing supplies the two radii and the base; reflecting the vertex keeps the same three lengths.

Height: 3.307 units. Area: 9.922 square units.

The whole passage

Greek and Latin: J. L. Heiberg, Euclidis opera omnia, vol. I (1883), pp. 52–55, public domain. Latin is Heiberg's nineteenth-century translation. English and teaching notes: Stoicheia, 2026, MIT. The original proof assumes all three strict inequalities; failed experimental givens do not alter the printed text.

1. A construction, with a condition

Ἐκ τριῶν εὐθειῶν, αἵ εἰσιν ἴσαι τρισὶ ταῖς δοθείσαις [εὐθείαις], τρίγωνον συστήσασθαι· δεῖ δὲ τὰς δύο τῆς λοιπῆς μείζονας εἶναι πάντῃ μεταλαμβανομένας [διὰ τὸ καὶ παντὸς τριγώνου τὰς δύο πλευρὰς τῆς λοιπῆς μείζονας εἶναι πάντῃ μεταλαμβανομένας].

Ex tribus rectis, quae tribus datis aequales sunt, triangulum construere (oportet autem duas reliqua maiores esse quoquo modo coniunctas).

To construct a triangle from three straight lines equal to three given [straight lines]. The two must be greater than the remaining one, however they are taken [because in every triangle, too, two sides are greater than the remaining side, however they are taken].

Language. συστήσασθαι / construere is an infinitive naming the task. δεῖ / oportet introduces a requirement. πάντῃ μεταλαμβανομένας / quoquo modo coniunctas means that every choice of two must be checked. Heiberg brackets the final Greek explanation; the Latin instead cites I.20 in an inline reference, omitted here.

Reason. I.20 proves the requirement for an existing triangle. I.22 now attempts the converse task: construct a triangle from lengths that meet that requirement.

2. Check all three pairings

Ἔστωσαν αἱ δοθεῖσαι τρεῖς εὐθεῖαι αἱ Α, Β, Γ, ὧν αἱ δύο τῆς λοιπῆς μείζονες ἔστωσαν πάντῃ μεταλαμβανόμεναι, αἱ μὲν Α, Β τῆς Γ, αἱ δὲ Α, Γ τῆς Β, καὶ ἔτι αἱ Β, Γ τῆς Α· δεῖ δὴ ἐκ τῶν ἴσων ταῖς Α, Β, Γ τρίγωνον συστήσασθαι.

Sint tres datae rectae Α, Β, Γ, quarum duae reliqua maiores sint quoquo modo coniunctae, Α + Β > Γ, Α + Γ > Β, Β + Γ > Α. oportet igitur ex rectis aequalibus rectis Α, Β, Γ triangulum construere.

Let Α, Β and Γ be the three given straight lines, and let any two be greater than the remaining one: Α and Β greater than Γ, Α and Γ greater than Β, and also Β and Γ greater than Α. We must construct a triangle from lines equal to Α, Β and Γ.

Language. ἔστωσαν / sint: ‘let them be’, plural. The genitive τῆς Γ follows the comparative μείζονες: ‘greater than Γ’. Here Α, Β and Γ name whole lengths, not the vertices of a triangle.

Reason. The givens include three strict inequalities. The experiments deliberately allow failures, but Euclid's proof below applies only while all three hold.

3. Place the lengths consecutively

Ἐκκείσθω τις εὐθεῖα ἡ ΔΕ πεπερασμένη μὲν κατὰ τὸ Δ ἄπειρος δὲ κατὰ τὸ Ε, καὶ κείσθω τῇ μὲν Α ἴση ἡ ΔΖ, τῇ δὲ Β ἴση ἡ ΖΗ, τῇ δὲ Γ ἴση ἡ ΗΘ.

sumatur recta ΔΕ terminata in Δ, uersus Ε autem infinita, et ponatur ΔΖ = Α, ΖΗ = Β, ΗΘ = Γ.

Set out a straight line ΔΕ, ending at Δ and extending without end towards Ε. Place ΔΖ equal to Α, ΖΗ equal to Β, and ΗΘ equal to Γ.

Language. πεπερασμένη μὲν … ἄπειρος δὲ contrasts an endpoint on one side with no endpoint on the other. κείσθω / ponatur commands the placement. The line on the screen is necessarily only a finite part of that ray.

Reason. The preceding length-transfer and cut-off constructions (I.2–3) supply the three copies. These are reused results, not a new permission to carry an arbitrary compass opening. ΖΗ, the middle copy, becomes the base.

4. Draw the first circle

καὶ κέντρῳ μὲν τῷ Ζ, διαστήματι δὲ τῷ ΖΔ κύκλος γεγράφθω ὁ ΔΚΛ·

et centro Ζ radio autem ΖΔ circulus describatur ΔΚΛ.

With centre Ζ and distance ΖΔ, let the circle ΔΚΛ be drawn.

Language. κέντρῳ … διαστήματι are datives specifying centre and distance; Latin uses centro … radio. γεγράφθω is a perfect passive imperative: ‘let it have been drawn’. Κ and Λ name the crossings anticipated in the successful construction.

Reason. Postulate 3 supplies the circle at an available centre through an available point. Every point of this circumference is the required distance Α from Ζ.

5. Draw the second; join at Κ

πάλιν κέντρῳ μὲν τῷ Η, διαστήματι δὲ τῷ ΗΘ κύκλος γεγράφθω ὁ ΚΛΘ, καὶ ἐπεζεύχθωσαν αἱ ΚΖ, ΚΗ· λέγω, ὅτι ἐκ τριῶν εὐθειῶν τῶν ἴσων ταῖς Α, Β, Γ τρίγωνον συνέσταται τὸ ΚΖΗ.

rursus centro Η radio autem ΗΘ circulus describatur ΚΛΘ, et ducantur ΚΖ, ΚΗ. dico, ex tribus rectis aequalibus rectis Α, Β, Γ triangulum constructum esse ΚΖΗ.

Again, with centre Η and distance ΗΘ, let the circle ΚΛΘ be drawn, and join ΚΖ and ΚΗ. I say that triangle ΚΖΗ has been constructed from three straight lines equal to Α, Β and Γ.

Language. πάλιν / rursus repeats the operation with another centre. ἐπεζεύχθωσαν / ducantur is plural: two lines are to be joined. συνέσταται says that the triangle has now been constructed. The interface separates drawing the second circle from joining the vertex.

Reason. Euclid proceeds directly to joining Κ. The existence of the common point needs justification beyond merely drawing two circles. The modern inequality and coordinate explanation below supplies a model, not a missing sentence in the ancient proof.

6. The first radius supplies Α

Ἐπεὶ γὰρ τὸ Ζ σημεῖον κέντρον ἐστὶ τοῦ ΔΚΛ κύκλου, ἴση ἐστὶν ἡ ΖΔ τῇ ΖΚ· ἀλλὰ ἡ ΖΔ τῇ Α ἐστιν ἴση· καὶ ἡ ΚΖ ἄρα τῇ Α ἐστιν ἴση.

nam quoniam Ζ punctum centrum est circuli ΔΚΛ, erit ΖΔ = ΖΚ; uerum ΖΔ = Α; quare etiam ΚΖ = Α.

Since point Ζ is the centre of circle ΔΚΛ, ΖΔ equals ΖΚ. But ΖΔ equals Α; therefore ΚΖ also equals Α.

Language. ἐπεὶ γάρ / nam quoniam begins the reason. ἀλλά / uerum supplies the previously established equality. ἄρα / quare signals the conclusion obtained by connecting them.

Reason. Radii of one circle are equal (definition 15 in this course). Common notion 1 carries the equality through the copied length ΖΔ. A measurement is a check of this drawing, not Euclid's reason.

7. The other radius supplies Γ

πάλιν, ἐπεὶ τὸ Η σημεῖον κέντρον ἐστὶ τοῦ ΛΚΘ κύκλου, ἴση ἐστὶν ἡ ΗΘ τῇ ΗΚ· ἀλλὰ ἡ ΗΘ τῇ Γ ἐστιν ἴση· καὶ ἡ ΚΗ ἄρα τῇ Γ ἐστιν ἴση.

rursus quoniam Η punctum centrum est circuli ΛΚΘ, erit ΗΘ = ΗΚ; uerum ΗΘ = Γ; quare etiam ΚΗ = Γ.

Again, since point Η is the centre of circle ΛΚΘ, ΗΘ equals ΗΚ. But ΗΘ equals Γ; therefore ΚΗ also equals Γ.

Language. The same reasoning returns with Η as centre and Γ as the given length. The circle is named ΛΚΘ here, rather than ΚΛΘ as in the construction; the transcription retains that change of order.

Reason. The second circumference certifies the second copied radius. A point on the first circle alone is not enough: this same Κ must also lie on the circle at Η.

8. Keep the middle copy as the base

ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ ἡ ΖΗ τῇ Β ἴση· αἱ τρεῖς ἄρα εὐθεῖαι αἱ ΚΖ, ΖΗ, ΗΚ τρισὶ ταῖς Α, Β, Γ ἴσαι εἰσίν.

et praeterea ΖΗ = Β. itaque tres rectae ΚΖ, ΖΗ, ΗΚ tribus Α, Β, Γ aequales sunt.

And ΖΗ also equals Β. The three straight lines ΚΖ, ΖΗ and ΗΚ therefore equal the three Α, Β and Γ.

Language. τρεῖς is nominative, the three lines being discussed; τρισί is dative, the three lengths to which they are equal. The Latin likewise contrasts tres and tribus.

Reason. ΖΗ was copied before either circle was drawn. The two circles supply the other two sides; they do not change the base to make the triangle fit.

9. What was required to be made

Ἐκ τριῶν ἄρα εὐθειῶν τῶν ΚΖ, ΖΗ, ΗΚ, αἵ εἰσιν ἴσαι τρισὶ ταῖς δοθείσαις εὐθείαις ταῖς Α, Β, Γ, τρίγωνον συνέσταται τὸ ΚΖΗ· ὅπερ ἔδει ποιῆσαι.

Ergo ex tribus rectis ΚΖ, ΖΗ, ΗΚ, quae tribus datis rectis Α, Β, Γ aequales sunt, triangulus constructus est ΚΖΗ; quod oportebat fieri.

Thus triangle ΚΖΗ has been constructed from the three straight lines ΚΖ, ΖΗ and ΗΚ, equal to the three given straight lines Α, Β and Γ: which was required to be made.

Language. ὅπερ ἔδει ποιῆσαι / quod oportebat fieri closes a construction. Compare ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι, ‘what was required to be shown’, at the end of I.20's theorem.

Reason. The conclusion belongs to the successful case with the original three strict inequalities. At a tangent there is only a straight configuration; when the circles miss, there is no common vertex at all.

Reading this edition

Line breaks, critical apparatus and inline Latin references are omitted. Greek ϑ is normalized to θ; Greek point labels and Heiberg's square brackets are retained. The English translates the Greek, including its bracketed explanation. ΔΕ is a ray; the drawing shows a finite part. T, P and Q are modern labels. The coordinate method establishes intersection in the real plane; it is not a derivation from Euclid's five postulates.
